title: Depressurizing Emotion: How to Calm a Hostile Written Conversation Using BIFF
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart addresses a near-universal hazard of working with people — parents, colleagues, bosses, students — over email: the hostile message that attacks your character. He introduces Bill Eddy's BIFF framework (Brief, Informative, Friendly, Firm) as a practical template for responding without escalating, walking through each element with concrete examples like closing with 'take care' or offering two specific phone slots to demonstrate firmness. He frames the underlying goal as repair rather than victory, arguing that 'winning' a hostile exchange is almost always a net loss for a working relationship you have to sustain. Stuart also offers two respectful caveats to Eddy's approach: he's wary of permanently labeling someone a 'High Conflict Person' since he believes most conflicts have some two-way origin worth reflecting on, and he explicitly carves out an exception for genuine abuse or gaslighting, where his advice about self-reflection and depersonalizing doesn't apply.
points: Stuart treats hostile communication as a structural certainty of working with people, not a personal failing — 'offending someone while working as an educator is a near mathematical certainty. It's not if, but when' — which reframes the skill as essential rather than optional.

The BIFF framework (Brief, Informative, Friendly, Firm) gives a concrete, repeatable structure for de-escalating written conflict, including the specific move of proposing a resolution deadline ('If I don't hear from you, I'll assume the issue is settled') rather than open-ended argument.
His invocation of John Wooden's character-versus-reputation distinction reframes BIFF responses as a character practice (defusing conflict before it ignites) rather than mere reputation management.

Stuart's caveat about 'High Conflict People' labeling pushes back against externalizing all blame onto the other party, arguing nearly every conflict includes some contribution from both sides worth reflecting on — while explicitly exempting genuine abuse or gaslighting from that self-reflection standard.
quotes: We educators are especially bound to run into hostile communications from time to time. With so many students, parents, colleagues, and bosses in our daily sphere, even the best of us are bound to find ourselves in conflict from time to time.
So when a hostile message does come in, my aim is repair — after all, winning battles like these is almost always a net loss. I don't want to win.

Keep it Brief. The more words, the more chances we create for communication to fail and the hostility cycle to deepen. If the parent is angry about a grading practice, no need to enumerate your philosophy on grading.

As the old, great teacher John Wooden sometimes said, your character is what you actually are while your reputation is what you appear to be. Attend to your character — which you're doing by defusing a hostile conversation before it ignites — and your reputation will take care of itself in due time.

I think it's possible to read a hostile communication impersonally, respond to it well, and also take to heart where we might be able to improve in the future. I can't think of a single conflict in my life where I didn't contribute at least one percent to the conflict's genesis.
Now, in circumstances of abuse, gaslighting, etc. — forget my caveats completely. We'll perform poorly, even in the inner work of morally engaging with a hostile other, when under too much pressure.
